Claude.notes: Exceptional opening module. The ChatGPT-November-2022 scene lands the problem (choosing matters) before the concept section introduces the three labs. Timeline, comparison grids, and the TIME/Sama citation are tightly woven. Capability delta is explicit: by end of module, a learner can map a lab's philosophy to its default behaviors.
Claude.topIssue: Lab 3 falls back to a generic 'explore Lesson 3 concepts' pattern (template leak) instead of a Claude-vs-RLHF comparison lab tailored to the lesson content.

Gemini.notes: Technical content is unusually tight for a Module 1. Attention Is All You Need (2017, 8 Google Brain authors), Anthropic founding team size (11), GPT-3 2020, Gemini 1.5 context all checked out. The Sama/TIME January 2023 citation is correct and specifically attributed. MoE explanation accurately captures routing semantics.
Gemini.topIssue: The quiz pins Claude 3's 200K as 'the largest at GA in early 2024' while treating Gemini 1.5's 1M as research-preview — correct at the moment but the distinction is quickly becoming stale and should be hedged.

Perplexity.notes: Historical framing is accurate but the model landscape has moved substantially since this content's late-2024 cap. Claude 3 Opus, GPT-4o, and Gemini 1.5 are treated as current frontier; in 2026 they are previous-generation. The 'natively multimodal from pretraining' distinction has largely collapsed as every major model is now natively multimodal.
Perplexity.topIssue: Capability deltas are framed against 2024's generation; a learner leaving this module in 2026 would reach for 'Claude 3 Opus' or 'GPT-4o' as if they were current frontier models rather than mid-tier legacy tiers.

Claude.notes: Technical arc from transformer → tokens → SFT → RLHF → multimodal is cleanly staged. The GPT-4o May 2024 demo opens the multimodal section well. The three-phase training explanation is one of the clearest versions of this material in the course.
Claude.topIssue: Lab 3 again uses the generic 'ask about a specific concept from Lesson 3' prompt — the template that should have been replaced with a module-specific RLHF behavior-probing lab. This appears in multiple modules and reads as unfinished.

Gemini.notes: Transformer and self-attention explanations are technically accurate at Advanced level. The tokenization lab prompt (emoji → how many tokens) is one of the better executable prompts in the course. SFT/RLHF/RBRM pipeline is faithful to InstructGPT and GPT-4 technical reports.
Gemini.topIssue: The 320ms audio-to-audio figure for GPT-4o is cited as a flat architecture property; in reality this is a best-case latency subject to many caveats (network, prompt length, voice mode variant). Should be hedged for technical accuracy.

Perplexity.notes: Entire module is framed around GPT-4o as the current flagship — a model that is now two major generations old in the GPT line. The RLHF→RLAIF/DPO shift in 2025 is not mentioned, which is a significant omission at Advanced level.
Perplexity.topIssue: A learner in 2026 doing the Lab asking 'why does GPT-4o add medical disclaimers' is asking about a legacy model. The lab should be framed around current-generation GPT behavior to be executable at the depth promised.

Claude.notes: The strongest narrative module in the course. The HHH triad is grounded in the Askell et al. framing, and the directness-vs-sycophancy section lands the behavioral insight through contrast with GPT. The French Revolution date-pushback lab is a near-perfect executable demonstration of Claude's calibrated disagreement.
Claude.topIssue: The 'When Claude's Directness Is an Asset — and When It Isn't' section is strong but could do more to let the learner arrive at the trade-off themselves rather than being told; it currently reads as presented rather than discovered.

Gemini.notes: CAI mechanics (self-critique against written principles, then preference training) are correctly described. HHH triad attribution is faithful. The claim that Claude's refusals are more consistent across paraphrases is backed by independent testing and holds up.
Gemini.topIssue: The 'Three-Tier Architecture' section describing Haiku/Sonnet/Opus is still correct for Claude 3 but has already been superseded by the Claude 4/5 tier structure, which this module doesn't mention.

Perplexity.notes: Constitutional AI as a mechanism remains correctly described and relevant. However, every concrete model reference (Claude 3 Opus, 200K context ceiling, Claude 2 → Claude 3 generational framing) is tied to a tier structure that has moved on twice since.
Perplexity.topIssue: The 'Choosing the Right Claude Tier' section is the most dated piece — Haiku/Sonnet/Opus 3 pricing and capability trade-offs no longer match what a learner would actually face in the Claude console in 2026.

Claude.notes: The Feb 2023 Bard demo controversy and the May 2024 AI Overviews glue-on-pizza incident both land the problem concretely before the concept section pivots to Google's structural advantages. Workspace/Vertex integration is explained clearly without hype.
Claude.topIssue: The 'When Gemini's Ecosystem Advantage Wins' vs. 'When GPT-4 or Claude Win Instead' pair reads a bit prescriptive — a case-based lab prompt would help learners arrive at the trade-off themselves.

Gemini.notes: Gemini 1.0/1.5 tier description and the Google Brain + DeepMind April 2023 consolidation are accurate. Both the Bard demo and AI Overviews incidents are summarized faithfully. 'Four-tier architecture' (Ultra/Pro/Flash/Nano) correctly described.
Gemini.topIssue: The Gemini 1.0 demo criticism is referenced accurately but could note that Google later confirmed the cuts explicitly in a tech-report footnote — a precision point for an Advanced-level audience.

Perplexity.notes: The May 2024 AI Overviews incident is still a defining Google-AI reference point and ages well. Gemini 1.5 Pro's 1M context is now baseline; the module doesn't reference Gemini 2.x which has been the production frontier for Google for most of 2025–2026.
Perplexity.topIssue: The 'Workspace: Gemini for Business and Enterprise' section lists capability tiers that have been renamed and rebundled multiple times — Gemini Enterprise, Gemini Business, Gemini Code Assist etc. The learner would not find these product names at the Google admin console today.

Claude.notes: The strongest conceptual module. Benchmark contamination, Goodhart's Law application to AI, and the HumanEval → EvalPlus story are each framed through a documented incident. Prompt-sensitivity testing section gives the learner a reusable research hygiene heuristic they can apply to any future model release.
Claude.topIssue: Narrative is slightly thinner than M3; stories open each lesson but tend to be short setups rather than extended scenes that create the problem.

Gemini.notes: Contamination mechanics, Goodhart's Law framing, LMSYS methodology, and HumanEval → EvalPlus (Liu et al. 2023) are described accurately with no overclaiming. The 'generic benchmarks don't predict your use case' framing is a strong technical message.
Gemini.topIssue: MMLU is treated as a canonical reference benchmark without flagging that top models have been saturating it since late 2024 — a learner at Advanced level should be told MMLU scores above ~88 carry little signal.

Perplexity.notes: The benchmark meta-points (contamination, Goodhart, LMSYS) age extremely well — the methodology concepts are durable even as the specific benchmarks churn. The best-aging module in the course.
Perplexity.topIssue: The specific benchmarks discussed (MMLU, HumanEval, HellaSwag) are now largely considered saturated; current frontier evals (SWE-Bench Verified, AIME, GPQA Diamond, HLE) are not mentioned, so the applied toolkit a learner leaves with is incomplete for 2026.

Claude.notes: The most operationally useful module. 'Lost in the middle', effective-vs-nominal context, model routing architectures, prompt-caching, and batch-API 50% discounts are all practical levers a production engineer would use. The Cursor IDE and Gemini 1.5 Pro launch scenes anchor each lesson in a real decision.
Claude.topIssue: Lab 3 again falls back to the template 'ask about a specific concept from Lesson 3' prompt, breaking the pattern established in Labs 1 and 2 that give concrete numerical scenarios.

Gemini.notes: TTFT vs tokens-per-second distinction is technically correct and useful. Lost-in-the-middle (Liu et al. 2023) and the effective-context vs. nominal-context distinction are accurately described. Caching and batching mechanics are faithful to the public API docs for all three providers.
Gemini.topIssue: The 'Why Gemini 1.5 Flash Leads on Raw Speed' section stakes a specific latency ranking that was true at a specific point in 2024 but is model-release-dependent — needs hedging as a snapshot.

Perplexity.notes: This is the most time-sensitive module in the course and it shows. API pricing, model-routing economics, and 'is Gemini Flash the cheapest?' answers have all moved substantially since 2024. The structural lessons (routing, caching, batching) are durable but every concrete number is stale.
Perplexity.topIssue: A learner running the Lab 1 prompt ('50,000 documents per day, walk me through daily cost on GPT-4o, GPT-4o mini, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 1.5 Flash') would be computing against legacy pricing on legacy models — the executable instructions are broken by currency drift.

Claude.notes: The applied-outcome capstone module. The 5-axis framework plus four concrete case studies (Morgan Stanley, Khanmigo, Quora Poe, Notion AI) is the strongest 'now you can do it' delivery in the course. Capability delta is explicit and defensible.
Claude.topIssue: Lab 3 reverts to the generic 'ask about Lesson 3' template, which weakens the case-study-driven lab pattern that works so well in Labs 1 and 2.

Gemini.notes: Morgan Stanley's Nov 2023 OpenAI deployment, Khan Academy's Khanmigo partnership, and the Poe/Notion AI product moves are all accurately described. The 5-axis framework (capability ceiling, context, latency, cost, safety posture) is a usable decision tool.
Gemini.topIssue: Case Study 4 ('high-volume content classification pipeline') prescribes GPT-4o mini and Claude 3.5 Haiku — model names that are now one generation back; the recommendation logic is still correct but the specific SKUs are not.

Perplexity.notes: The decision framework itself (5-axis, workload-to-model mapping) ages well. But every case study is tied to 2023–2024 deployments and specific model SKUs that have been superseded. Morgan Stanley has since broadened their stack beyond pure OpenAI, which the module doesn't reflect.
Perplexity.topIssue: The 'Side-by-Side Decision Logic' table recommends Claude 3.5 vs. GPT-4o vs. Gemini 1.5 Pro by task — a learner in 2026 making a procurement decision from this table would be deciding between the wrong three options.

Claude.notes: Good closing module. The 'Claude picks up a mouse' Oct 2024 scene for computer use, the Sept 2024 o1 reasoning-model scene, and the agent safety dimension land as story-first problem framings. The 'how to evaluate a new model release' section is a durable skill rather than a snapshot.
Claude.topIssue: The 'Strategic Advice for Professionals' closing section is largely told-at rather than discovered — a reflection prompt instead of a told conclusion would land the capability transfer harder.

Gemini.notes: o1 chain-of-thought reasoning (Sept 2024), o3 preview (Dec 2024), Claude Computer Use (Oct 2024), and the agent safety dimension are each described accurately. The 'primary sources' section (tech reports, model cards, independent evals) is sound methodological guidance.
Gemini.topIssue: The reasoning-model section describes o1-style test-time compute as a differentiator; by 2026 every frontier lab has shipped reasoning-mode models and the differentiator has dissolved — this isn't flagged.

Perplexity.notes: Of the eight modules this one ages the best because it is explicitly framed as 'the frontier is moving' and sets expectations of churn. However, the specific timeline caps at Dec 2024 (o3 preview, Claude 3.5 Sonnet) and misses the GPT-5 / Claude 4 / Claude 5 / Gemini 2.x / Gemini 3 cycles that followed.
Perplexity.topIssue: Lab 4 asks the learner to evaluate 'a new model that just launched claiming to beat GPT-4o on every benchmark' — the GPT-4o anchor is no longer the comparison frontier a 2026 buyer would use, which pulls down the lab's executability.
